section: Face Deblurring using Dual Camera Fusion on Mobile Phones
text: Motion blur of fast-moving subjects is a longstanding problem in photography and very common on mobile phones due to limited light collection efficiency, particularly in low-light conditions. While we have witnessed great progress in image deblurring in recent years, most methods require significant computational power and have limitations in processing highresolution photos with severe local motions. To this end, we develop a novel face deblurring system based on the dual camera fusion technique for mobile phones. The system detects subject motion to dynamically enable a reference camera, e.g., ultrawide angle camera commonly available on recent premium phones, and captures an auxiliary photo with faster shutter settings. While the main shot is low noise but blurry (Figure 1(a)), the reference shot is sharp but noisy (Figure 1(b)). We learn ML models to align and fuse these two shots and output a clear photo without motion blur (Figure 1(c)). Our algorithm runs efficiently on Google Pixel 6, which takes 463 ms overhead per shot.

text:
Recovering sharp details from blurry faces through post-capture processing is fundamentally challenging. Blind deconvolution methods often model motion blur as a global or slowly-varying local kernels [Ren et al . 2016; Yang and Ji 2019], and cannot handle face motions that may contain non-rigid and out-of-plane movements, saturation at eye highlights, camera ISP non-linearity, lens aberration, and self-occlusion between hairs and facial landmarks. Deep learning methods using a single image [Cho et al . 2021; Nah et al . 2017], a multi-frame burst [Aittala and Durand 2018], or a video sequence [Son et al . 2021; Su et al . 2017] have made significant progresses over the years. However, high-quality solutions on highresolution data require expensive computation that is prohibitive on mobile phones with limited memory and processing budget.
This paper describes a system to deblur faces of moving subjects captured by handheld mobile phones. We tailor the system to faces given its importance in mobile photography. Our system, which launched to the public as Face Unblur on Google Pixel 6 smartphones, aims to achieve the following goals:

- Reliably produce high-quality, high-resolution (2.3MP), realisticlooking, and artifact-free deblur results on moving subjects in the wild. We handle any form of face motion in real-world, where the motion blur size can reach hundreds of pixels.
- Require no additional users inputs other than pressing the shutter button. The system detects motion blur, identifies the blurry areas, and applies deblurring automatically.
- Run on mobile phone at interactive rate. In other words, users see the result immediately after the photo is taken.
- Operate within the power, memory, and computation budget provided by the SoC on Google Pixel 6.
- Support zero-shutter lag capture for motion subject. The deblurring is applied to the moment that the user intends to capture, not nearby frames.

text: Our solution is built on (1) the heterogeneous dual camera system adopted by the majority of phone vendors, i.e., a wide-angle main camera and a secondary ultrawide-angle camera, denoted as W and UW throughout this paper, and (2) the ability to synchronize timestamp, auto-exposure, and auto white-balancing between W and UW cameras offered by most smartphones. When the user captures a moving subject using the main W camera, our system captures a synchronized reference raw using the UW camera at a faster shutter speed to acquire sharp but noisy facial details. The main W and reference UW shots exhibit different viewpoint and sensor characteristics, e.g., noise, gain, color, etc. We train deep CNNs to align and fuse the low noise but blurry linear RAW from W, and noisy but sharp linear RAW from UW, generating a clean and sharp linear raw of the face region from the W 's point of view (Section 3). The fused linear RAW is then fed to a standard image processing pipeline to output the tone-mapped result.

Compared to the alternative that takes long and short exposure frames from the same camera, our dual camera approach leverages temporal synchronization to greatly improve the quality of image alignment between W and UW .
However, dual W and UW streaming consumes prohibitively high power and memory footprint. To reduce the amortized power, we propose an adaptive stream system to dynamically enable and disable the UW sensor based on real-time motion analysis. We integrate the algorithm into the camera driver to avoid excessive activation delay (Section 4) . Finally, we describe the requirements of the camera image signal processing pipeline to enable our system (Section 5).

text: Section 6 evaluates our deblur results over 1783 images exhibiting motions in daily tasks, such as jumping, walking, and exercising, containing subjects of diverse skin color, gender, and face poses. The inputs are challenging and consist of local, non-rigid, and large motion, where blur kernel may reach up to hundreds of pixels. We compare our results against state-of-the-art methods in single-image, multi-frame, face-specific, and video-based deblurring papers, as well as commercial products such as iPhone13 Pro, Shake Reduction filter in Adobe PhotoShop, and Samsung Gallery's Remaster function. Our method achieves higher scores on no-reference image quality metrics and generates results that look visually more pleasing. Our images used for comparisons in Section 6 are available at the project website 1 . To the best of our knowledge, our system is the first practical face deblur solution that runs on mobile phones.

text: Conventional methods typically rely on the MAP optimization framework [Cho and Lee 2009; Fergus et al . 2006; Shan et al . 2008; Xu and Jia 2010] and natural image priors [Krishnan et al . 2011; Lai et al . 2015; Pan et al . 2016b; Sun et al . 2013; Xu et al . 2013] for single-image blind deblurring. text: With the advance of deep learning techniques in recent years, several learning-based approaches adopt deep CNNs for motion deblurring. Early methods train CNNs to predict local blur kernels [Gong et al . 2017; Sun et al . 2015] or learn image priors [Li et al . 2018], but still involve conventional optimization-based framework to deblur images. Recent approaches train end-to-end CNNs for single-image debluring by exploring different architecture designs [Cho et al . 2021; Gao et al . 2019; Kaufman and Fattal 2020; Li et al . 2020; Nah et al . 2017; Suin et al . 2020; Tao et al . 2018; Zamir et al . 2021; Zhang et al . 2019, 2020] or GAN-based training [Kupyn et al . 2018, 2019]. While state-of-the-art methods achieve great performance on benchmark datasets (e.g., GoPro [Nah et al . 2017] and RealBlur [Rim et al .

Optimization-based approaches handle saturation by excluding saturated pixels [Dong et al . 2017; Pan et al . 2016a; Whyte et al . 2014] or estimating blur kernels from light streaks [Hu et al . 2014]. We found that our model trained on synthetic data may not be able to remove saturated light streaks and leave undesired ringing artifacts (see Figure 17). Therefore, we add synthetic light streaks to our training data and find this simple data augmentation sufficient to remove saturated blur streaks.

text: As single-image deblurring is a challenging ill-posed problem, several methods have exploited additional input images for deblurring. Multi-frame deblurring approaches merge a burst of images via Fourier burst accumulation [Delbracio and Sapiro 2015a] or deep CNNs [Aittala and Durand 2018]. Early video deblurring methods use optical flow to model linear motion blur [Hyun Kim and Mu Lee

text: 2015; Ren et al . 2017] or merge sharp pixels or patches from neighboring frames [Cho et al . 2012; Delbracio and Sapiro 2015b]. Recent learning-based approaches learn to aggregate information from neighboring frames using optical flow [Su et al . 2017], recurrent networks [Hyun Kim et al . 2017; Nah et al . 2019; Son et al . 2021; Zhou et al . 2019], spatial-temporal transformers [Kim et al . 2018], deformable convolutions [Wang et al . 2019], and multi-patch architectures [Deng et al . 2021]. Our system captures W and UW raw bursts consisting of 7 − 9 frames and uses the robust local alignment in [Hasinoff et al . 2016] to merge raw frames to a single linear image before deblurring. The robust local alignment step avoids additional blur in the raw-merging step. Compared to deblurring on raw burst frames, deblurring on the merged linear image avoids the challenging temporal alignment and excessive memory cost.

text: Reference-based approaches take a pair of blurry and sharp, shortexposed images as inputs [Chang et al . 2021; Gu et al . 2020; Yuan et al. 2007; Zhuo et al. 2010]. Early approaches adopt conventional Richardson–Lucy deconvolution [Yuan et al . 2007] or MAP framework [Zhuo et al . 2010] to estimate a blur kernel for deblurring. These methods assume the input and reference images are wellaligned, and motion blur is spatially-invariant i.e., a global blur kernel exists. The assumption does not apply to dynamic subject motions in our problem. Gu et al. [2020] use optical flow to align the noisy reference image and build GMM priors to model the sharp latent image. This work requires expensive iterative optimization (10+ minutes as reported in [Gu et al . 2020]), which makes it difficult to run efficiently on mobile devices. Chang et al. [2021] learns CNNs to align and fuse long and short exposure frames for deblurring. They capture frames sequentially, which makes alignment challenging for fast-moving subjects that often involve non-rigid motion.

text: Compared to natural images, face images are highly structural and consist of rich semantic information such as facial contours and landmarks. Conventional optimization approaches [Hacohen et al . 2013; Pan et al . 2014] search for a reference face to guide the image deblurring. These methods often require careful alignment between the blurry and reference images to estimate accurate blur kernels. Recent CNN-based approaches learn semantic labels [Shen et al . 2018, 2020; Yasarla et al . 2020], facial sketches [Lin et al . 2020], or 3D facial reconstructions [Ren et al . 2019] for deblurring. However, such methods based on facial priors could fail when a subject wears a mask (e.g., the third example in Figure 12). Instead of learning face priors or searching for a reference face from an external database, we propose an end-to-end system that concurrently captures a sharp reference face and learns ML models to fuse the blurry and reference images.

text: Our fusion algorithm takes two images as input, where we treat W as the source and UW as the reference image. When subject motion is detected, we enable dual camera streaming to concurrently capture W and UW raw bursts [Hasinoff et al . 2016]. The exposure time of W is determined by the auto-exposure algorithm for the optimal SNR and sharpness performance in averaged cases, but is usually too long for fast-moving subjects, and leads to blurry faces. The UW image is deliberately captured at a higher shutter speed than W to minimize motion blur, at the cost of more noise and artifacts. We lock the UW's exposure time to be 1 𝑁 of W's exposure time. We test 𝑁 = 2 and 𝑁 = 4 in this paper. Note that our system design is independent of the choice of raw burst capture. We adopt the raw capture in our pipeline since many phones employ raw burst capture in the post-capture processing pipeline for high-dynamicrange enhancements.

text: Model architecture. Our FusionNet illustrated in Figure 24 has N-level pyramids for the encoder and decoder. At each level, the encoder block uses 1 Conv layer, followed by another Conv that uses a stride of 2 to downsample the features by 2. The decoder block at each layer uses 2 Conv layers followed by a bilinear upsampling layer to upsample the features. Except the output layer, each Conv layer is followed by a ReLU activation layer. In the first level, the encoder extracts features from the source image and downsamples them by 2×. In the second level, we concatenate the warped reference image, face mask, and occlusion mask as inputs and extract reference features. The features from source and reference are fused and become the input features to the second pyramid level. In the last decoder block, the upsampled feature is fused with the source feature (before downsampling). We apply another Conv layer to generate a 3-channel image as the output.

text: Our fusion pipeline contains 3 ML models: optical flow (PWC-Net), fusion deblur (FusionNet), and subject segmentation (UNet). To deploy them on the mobile phone, we convert the models into TensorFlow lite format [Abadi et al . 2016] and delegate inference to the accelerators. text: Our algorithm requires a mobile phone to stream both W and UWcameras. However, continuously streaming bothWand UWcamera consumes high power (+400 mW) unsustainable for thermal status. Moreover, it requires a large additional memory footprint (+160 MB). To save amortized power, we present an adaptive stream system that dynamically enables and disables UW camera based on real-time motion analysis, as illustrated in Figure 10. Our adaptive streaming system determines whether the subject in the frame 𝑡 demonstrates excessive motion that leads to motion blur, and, if so, streams UW at 𝑡 + 1 to capture the short-exposed reference. The motion analysis and decision need to be made within the duration of 1-frame, i.e., 33ms when the camera streams at 30 FPS. To meet the real-time requirement, we propose a lightweight SVM model that takes feature vectors from camera metadata relevant to motion blur and outputs a binary flag indicating whether to turn on UW camera. We now describe our SVM model and implementation for mobile camera systems.

Comparisons with academic approaches. We compare our results to the recent deblurring approaches listed below:
- Single-image: DeblurGAN-v2 [Kupyn et al . 2019], MPRNet [Zamir et al. 2021], and MIMO-UNet+ [Cho et al. 2021].

Note that the existing approaches are typically trained on 8-bit gamma images, e.g., GoPro dataset [Nah et al . 2017], while our training images are 16-bit linear before any tone-mappings. It is nontrivial to re-train or fine-tune existing models with our training data. Therefore, we use the pre-trained model released by the authors of each method for fair comparisons.

Latency and memory. We implement our system on Google Pixel 6 released in 2021. The SoC consists of Mali-G78 GPU, Cortex multi-core, and an NPU. The latency overhead is 463ms, which consists of preprocessing, alignment, fusion, and the Polyblur in post-processing, as reported in Table 2. We exclude merging W burst raw and tone-mapping from the overhead since they are already required in the single camera processing without our fusion deblur. Merging UW burst raw is scheduled concurrently with merging W burst and does not take additional latency. Our system's peak memory usage happens at the FusionNet inference stage, which takes an extra 264 MB compared to the peak memory usage in single camera processing pipeline.
Power. When dual camera streaming at 30 FPS, the power overhead is 468mW, which splits between power rail from UW sensor (332mW) and SoC (136mW) for RAW data transaction between DRAM and the UW camera system. On average, our adaptive system streams UW 1.8% of the camera session time, which results in 8.4mW amortized power cost.

In this section, we validate the contributions of key design choices of our fusion algorithm, including the color-consistency loss, synthetic light streaks in training data generation, and compare our method with single-image deblurring. Additional ablation analysis are provided in the supplementary material, including analysis on the perceptual loss, mask smoothing, Polyblur, optical flow, and how our FusionNet utilizes each input for deblurring.
Color-consistency loss. As W and UW use different camera sensors, there will be inevitable color mismatch even after our color matching and AE synchronization. Without the color-consistency loss Lcolor, inconsistent color may be transferred from the reference image to the fusion result, such as green color on the hair of the two examples in Figure 15. By training with the color-consistency loss, our FusionNet learns to keep the color of the source image after deblurring.

The quality of our fusion results mainly depends on the quality of UW images. Our method may fail to restore a clear face under the following situations: 1) extreme low-light: As the UW image is captured at a faster exposure time of W, the UW image may appear excessively noisy under the extreme low-light scenes. Our FusionNet may transfer the noise from the reference image and lead to painterly artifacts, as shown in Figure 18. 2) Small face: When the face is too small, UW may not be able to capture facial details for restoration, as shown in Figure 19. In this work, we have presented a robust system to address motion blur on faces in portrait photography. Our system runs efficiently on Google Pixel 6 smartphones at the capturing time and produces visually more pleasing results than state-of-the-art single-image, multi-frame, video, and face-specific deblurring methods through extensive evaluations. By leveraging the dual camera system available on major premium phones, we have shown that combining optical flow for alignment, residual UNet for image fusion, and training on synthetic data can address the challenges that would be difficult to approach through a single camera setup. We have specified a list of system requirements including adaptive stream and camera ISP to make the dual camera fusion practical on mobile devices. We hope our work encourages further progress on reference-based image deblurring.

Perceptual loss. Without the perceptual loss L vgg , our deblurred results often look overly smooth. Since motion blur cannot be completely removed, the results contain ringing or blurriness around the eyeglasses frame, as shown in Figure 20(b). By training with the perceptual loss, our FusionNet generates sharper results with richer facial details, as shown in Figure 20(c).
Face mask smoothing. We apply an alpha blending to blend our deblurred face with the full-resolution source image. Without the mask boundary smoothing, a clear border is visible in the deblurred image, as shown in Figure 21. The smoothed mask for alpha blending helps to avoid such a sharp transition.
Polyblur. As our fusion results may look overly-smooth, we adopt the Polyblur [Delbracio et al . 2021] method to enhance the sharpness. Polyblur mainly removes mild blur caused by lens blur or small out-of-focus, while our FusionNet can reduce large motion blur caused by subject motion. Figure 22 shows an example that Polyblur improves the detail sharpness around the eyes.

text: From our analysis, the FusionNet does not blindly copy everything from the reference image to the output. Instead, the FusionNet learns to apply fusion only when the source and reference have correspondences, e.g., the same face, within the face mask. While using occlusion mask could sacrifice the sharpness on face boundary, it is crucial to prevent any unnatural artifacts in the results. Minimizing artifacts is an important goal of our system, and we are willing to be conservative in the amount of sharpening.
